title: Started at 12, Now 300,000 Strong: India's Children-Led Digital Art Museum
excerpt: The Children's Art Museum of India, launched by two teenagers in 2022, has grown into a 300,000-member community of young artists — and it has never raised a rupee of investor funding.
body:
• Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta started CAMI in 2022 — when they were 12 and 14 — asking one question: what happens to a child's painting after it is made?
  • Four years on, the digital platform counts more than 300,000 members, over 20,000 submitted artworks and 1 million-plus website visitors across 200 cities and towns in India.
  • The initiative remains bootstrapped with no investor funding, run on a "by the children, for the children, of the children" ethos.
  • CAMI now builds learning resources on traditional Indian art forms and plans to deepen its international community and interactive museum experiences.

A children's painting usually lives a short public life: a few days on a wall or a refrigerator door, some praise from parents, then a drawer. Four years ago, two schoolchildren in Gurugram decided that ending was not good enough. Their answer — the Children's Art Museum of India (CAMI), a digital museum where children's artwork is displayed, seen and taken seriously — has since grown into a community of more than 300,000 members.

Two kids, one question

Krish Nawal was 12 and Manya Roongta was 14 when they launched CAMI in 2022, as YourStory reports. The spark came during the COVID-19 pandemic, when Krish noticed that professional artists had museums, galleries and digital platforms — while there were almost no spaces designed specifically for children to share their work beyond submitting it and forgetting it.

"My interest in art was never limited to learning how to draw or paint," Krish told YourStory. "Over time, I became more interested in the question of what could be created around art. Every child sees the same subject differently, and that idea became central to CAMI." The idea began without an elaborate business plan. "We didn't start CAMI thinking that it would one day become a large organisation. We simply wanted a child to see their own painting in a museum and feel that this space belonged to them too."

From neighbourhood project to a national platform

The start was modest: asking friends to share their paintings. Growth came through schools, young ambassadors and creative programmes, and the numbers now tell the story. More than 20,000 paintings and artworks have been submitted to the platform, its website has drawn over a million visitors, and the community has reached more than 200 cities and towns across India.

The Mint's 2023 reporting, when the platform was still young, already captured its logic: CAMI operates as a free online art platform where children aged 3 and above can upload work after the founders review it for appropriateness, with monthly art challenges and learning resources built in. "We saw this as a space where kids from all over the world could feel inspired by each other," Krish said then — a vision that has since scaled far beyond its neighbourhood beginnings.

Context and background

The gap CAMI addressed was real. In India, art in schools is still often treated as an extra-curricular activity rather than a core part of learning, and access to quality art programmes, trained teachers and creative resources is uneven. The platform has responded with digital learning material — including hundreds of videos focused on traditional Indian art forms — aimed not just at improving children's drawing but at connecting them with India's cultural heritage.

Crucially, CAMI has remained bootstrapped since its inception, raising no investor funding. Early expenses for hosting, design and technology were covered through family backing and available resources. "We wanted to keep access simple and open to as many children as possible from the beginning," Krish said. "Our first goal was to understand whether children and schools would adopt the idea. So we focused first on usefulness and participation."

"Children don't always need another competition. They need a space where their creativity can simply be seen."

— Krish Nawal, co-founder, CAMI

Impact and analysis

CAMI's trajectory says something about both art education and young entrepreneurship. The recognition has come at national and international levels — the Global Youth Award for Creative Innovation, the Bower School of Entrepreneurship's Top 18 Under 18 Entrepreneurship Award, and a speaking slot at the MuseumNext Digital Museums Conference — but the operating discipline is the more interesting part.

The founders have had to manage, alongside school, the problems of any fast-growing platform: maintaining quality at scale, ensuring children's safety online, and earning institutional trust. "When we started, we were very young, and earning trust was our biggest challenge," Krish admitted. "Later, we had to constantly focus on quality and the safety of children as well." The choice to stay bootstrapped meant the metric of success stayed community-driven: how many children could share their creativity, not how much revenue followed.

Diaspora angle

For Indian-origin families abroad, CAMI is a natural bridge. Children in the diaspora can submit artwork, take part in challenges, and learn about traditional Indian art forms through its resources — a way of engaging with Indian cultural heritage that asks for nothing more than a painting and an internet connection.

What's next

Krish wants CAMI to go beyond a website where children upload paintings: expanding its school network, strengthening its international community and building more interactive museum experiences, including experiments with AI and virtual worlds. The guardrail, he says, stays the same — a child's opportunities should not depend on whether they live in a large city or a small town. "Every child doesn't have to become an artist. But every child should feel that their creativity has value."
